content.overview: BNS s. 31 — Communication made in good faith.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Communication made in good faith. BNS restatement of IPC 93. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 93. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 31 is the rule on “Communication made in good faith”. The section provides that no communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 31 exists so that “Communication made in good faith” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
31. No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person

Essential ingredients
1. No communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A, a surgeon, in good faith, communicates to a patient his opinion that he cannot live. The patient dies in consequence of the shock. A has committed no offence, though he knew it to be likely that the communication might cause the patient’s death

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 31 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:

Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 31 in a vacuum.

learningObjectives: Understand the scope of BNS s. 31 protecting communications made in good faith.
Analyze the requirement that the communication must be made for the benefit of the person.
Examine the doctor-patient relationship and professional disclosures causing shock.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 31 provides that no communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, if it is made for the benefit of that person.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: A truthful communication delivered in good faith for the recipient's benefit does not constitute an offence, even if the psychological or physical shock of receiving the news results in injury or death.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 31 (corresponding to IPC s. 93).
Condition 1: Communication must be made in 'good faith' (due care and attention under s. 2(11)).
Condition 2: Must be made 'for the benefit of that person'.
Harm covered: Any harm (including emotional shock, nervous breakdown, heart attack) resulting from the communication.
essentialIngredients: A communication was made by the doer to a person.
The communication was made in good faith.
The communication was made for the benefit of the recipient.
Harm resulted to the recipient from that communication.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 31 protects individuals who have a duty or reasonable justification to convey grave, distressing news to another for that person's benefit. The most common illustration is a medical doctor who informs a patient that their illness is terminal, in order to allow the patient to settle affairs or seek specialized care. If the patient suffers a fatal heart attack from the shock, the doctor is not criminally liable for manslaughter or negligence because the disclosure was made in good faith for the patient's benefit. If the communication is made with malicious intent or recklessly without medical necessity, s. 31 does not apply.
examples: Teaching example (Doctor informing patient): A doctor in good faith informs a patient that he has an inoperable aortic aneurysm and cannot live long, so that he may write his will and manage his treatment. The patient dies of heart failure due to shock. The doctor is protected under s. 31.

Teaching example (Malicious shock): A rival falsely and maliciously tells an elderly person that his only son was killed in an accident, intending to cause severe distress. The father suffers a stroke. Section 31 does not apply because the statement was neither true, nor in good faith, nor for the person's benefit.
distinctions: Communication for benefit vs Malicious infliction of nervous shock: Section 31 requires genuine good faith for the recipient's benefit; malicious or cruel revelations are unprotected.
Section 31 vs Defamation exceptions: Section 31 protects against harm to the recipient; Defamation exceptions protect communication to third parties.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a physician who disclosed a diagnosis of terminal cancer to a patient who subsequently suffered fatal shock is criminally liable.
Rule: BNS s. 31 provides that communications made in good faith for the recipient's benefit do not constitute an offence.
Application: Establish that the diagnosis was medically verified, communicated professionally with due care, and intended to enable the patient to arrange urgent medical and personal affairs.
Conclusion: Section 31 applies; the physician is exempt from liability.
